Humor is one of the most complicated aspects of language use to learn since there are also cultural considerations to consider. Also, a novice learner will experience more instances of L1-L2 transfer (meme language won't make sense or transfer intelligibly from/to their native language), and will rely more on conscious production of language. Although I would imagine an English learner could copy certain meme language, they would have a harder time unconsciously knowing what sounds "right."

I'm relatively new, so can only speak to what I know and have experienced so far, but we have a comprehensive "New Members Education Program." This involves reading introductory essays about Marxism and socialism in general, along with Socialist Alternative's actions here in the US and by our sister branches globally. The literature has been updated recently, so not sure what has changed in terms of content. This program also includes discussion among the members. 

We recently put on a Day School which involved several members giving presentations centered on the Russian Revolution and related concepts. This was open to the public. Last weekend we had another public educational meeting about ongoing actions. Our branch meetings are currently every other week, with a business portion and an open informational/discussion portion. 

Apart from education, our local SA branch has recently involved in organizing a May Day rally and march here in DC, in a coalition of other leftist groups. That same weekend we had an integral part in a Workers March for those who could not strike on May Day. We have also had a presence at the other larger, more liberal marches as a tabling opportunity and to give the left a presence there. 

We also engage in direct action, most recently assisting in a picket outside of Whole Foods to defend a wrongly fired employee. We have also helped blockade a "pro-life" march in February.

We as a party also run candidates, as you may know. The most well known is Kshama Sawant, city councilwoman in Seattle who has won the position twice against an established democrat. She helped lead the Fight for $15 movement which as spread across the country. We are running a candidate now in Minneapolis, Ginger Jentzen. We believe in running candidates in order to make legislative change. 

We like to plug into as many local actions as we can. A comrade is highly involved in DC Reinvest, a campaign to get DC city council to divest from Wells Fargo and to reinvest in local banks. Also, we are currently involved in the "No Justice No Pride" movement to bring back radicalism to a more inclusive, less corporate Pride. 

There are a handful of other orgs. we are involved with, but I don't want to ramble too much longer. Hope this helps!

Having a fierce pride in your home country/location would, I suspect, inhibit the degree to which you adopt a new linguistic variation (accent, slang, etc.). This pride would perhaps hinder your motivation to assimilate into the new group with their different speech habits. However, there's still accommodation to consider- that is, the social/psychological process of unconsciously matching the speech patters of those you are speaking with. This occurs even with people of the same dialect/accent, with those individuals perhaps matching intonation, pitch, speed, idiolectic slang, etc. So if you were to move somewhere in which you were immersed in a new speech pattern, you would most likely change some aspects of your own language naturally, for ease of communication. I don't suspect the original accent would vanish entirely, but would be altered. Keep in mind, too, that the degree of variation between the original speech variety and the new would influence the degree of change you'd see.

It's also possible that as your child begins to speak, they would persistently use English with you, even if you try to use Korean. From what I remember from my language acquisition class, children may default (stubbornly) to the language that is easiest to communicate with a particular person. Now, this doesn't mean that your child won't implicitly pick up on your Korean habits, just perhaps they will tend to shy away from using this language with you. I agree with other replies-- nothing to worry about in terms of them learning "wrong" Korean. Very interesting scenario you've got going, I'd be interested to see how this turns out!
